questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The instruction that covers two operations
questions.learningObjective: Spot one instruction covering two actions
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, a step reads 'Pour and level the concrete in one pass'. Why is this problematic?

options.text: It combines two operations into one instruction.

questions.explanation: Pouring and leveling are distinct operations. Combining them risks skipping one. Thickness, length, and necessity are separate concerns.

stimulus.body: Step 3: Install the vapour barrier on the warm side of the wall. Note: In cold climates, place the barrier on the cold side to prevent condensation. The brief offers no guidance on which rule applies.

questions.stem: In an architect's brief, what is the problem?

questions.explanation: The note gives a rule that opposes the step and offers no resolution. The barrier is required, and length or climate existence are not the issue.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Who is expected to check the work
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, the inspection section says 'Verify the work' but names no one. Why does this matter?

answer.exemplar: Without a named checker, no one is accountable, so verification may be skipped or assumed done, and defects can pass into the next stage.

questions.explanation: A check without an owner is often skipped. Naming the checker creates accountability and prevents defects from propagating.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Change between two editions of a guide
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, edition 8 changes the wind pressure values but keeps the same step numbers. What is the risk?

options.text: Readers may use old pressures with new steps.

questions.explanation: When pressure values change but step numbers stay the same, readers can mix old and new content. Numbering, length, and fault are separate concerns.
questions.hint: Can old and new content be mixed?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A claim about ease that a reader will test
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, a step says 'This truss is easy to lift'. Why is this risky?

options.text: Ease is subjective and readers may disagree.

questions.explanation: An ease claim is subjective and invites dispute. It does not prove weight, and length or necessity are separate.

questions.topic: Ambiguity in check the frame
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, a step says 'Check the wall'. What is ambiguous?

options.text: Which wall and what to check are unspecified.

questions.explanation: 'Check the wall' names no wall and no criterion. Size, necessity, and length are separate concerns.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The measurement the reader must supply

stimulus.body: Step 11: Cut the beam to the required span. Step 12: Fit the support. Step 13: Bolt the connection. The brief names no dimensions anywhere.

questions.stem: In an architect's brief, which measurement must the reader supply?

options.text: None, because the steps are standard.

questions.explanation: Step 11 says 'required span' but names no dimension, so the reader must supply it. The other steps also lack dimensions but the beam span is the first missing measurement. Standard sizes are not stated.
questions.hint: Which step first lacks a number?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The instruction that covers two operations
questions.learningObjective: Spot one instruction covering two actions
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, a step reads 'Pour and finish the slab in one pass'. Why is this problematic?

options.text: It combines two operations into one instruction.

questions.explanation: Pouring and finishing are distinct operations. Combining them risks skipping one. Thickness, length, and necessity are separate concerns.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A note that contradicts a step
questions.learningObjective: Detect a contradiction between note and step

stimulus.body: Step 10: Install the flashing before the cladding. Note: Flashing should be installed after cladding to overlap correctly. The brief offers no guidance on which order to use.

questions.stem: In an architect's brief, what is the problem?

options.text: The note contradicts the step without resolving it.

questions.explanation: The note gives an order that opposes the step and offers no resolution. Flashing is required, and length or overlap are not the issue.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Who is expected to check the work
questions.stem: In an architect's brief, the inspection section says 'Verify the squareness' but names no one. Why does this matter?

answer.exemplar: Without a named checker, no one is accountable, so verification may be skipped or assumed done, and defects can pass into the next stage.

questions.explanation: A check without an owner is often skipped. Naming the checker creates accountability and prevents defects from propagating.
